extracted.intended_audience: Practitioners (attorneys) who represent trademark applicants before the USPTO, and their non‑practitioner staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and expectations for trademark practitioners practicing before the USPTO, especially regarding electronic signatures, delegation, diligence, and filings (e.g., declarations) that the Office relies upon. Includes discipline and publication consequences for failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark electronic signature requirements (37 C.F.R. § 2.193; TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark filings must be personally signed; the person identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verbatim guidance from the Order/TMEP: "All documents must be personally signed. 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a)(1), (c)(1), 11.18(a). The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory. Just as signing the name of another person on paper does not serve as the signature of the person whose name is written, typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person." (See TMEP § 611.01(c) and 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a)(2),(c),(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on non‑practitioner assistants signing for named signatories
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑practitioner assistants (paralegals, legal assistants, secretaries) may not sign or enter the name/electronic signature of an attorney or other authorized signatory on trademark filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order explicitly states that "typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person" and cites TMEP and prior decisions (In re Dermahose Inc.; In re Cowan) to reinforce that another person may not sign the name of a practitioner on either paper or electronically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to provide diligent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an ethical obligation to provide diligent representation to clients; failing to act with reasonable diligence can result in discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners may delegate tasks to non‑practitioner paraprofessionals, but when delegating the practitioner is required to confirm the task is performed in compliance with USPTO rules. The Order notes a practitioner "may be disciplined for failing to act diligently by, among other things, delegating the task of obtaining client signatures to non‑practitioner assistants, and not reasonably ensuring that the task was being carried out in compliance with the USPTO trademark signature rules."

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation not to engage in conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are reasonably expected not to file, or allow to be filed, trademark documents that are improperly signed, because such conduct prejudices the administration of the USPTO trademark registration system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order explains improperly signed documents may lead to registrations on the USPTO register, undermine public reliance on the register, and adversely affect the integrity of the federal trademark registration process. Filing or allowing improperly signed declarations or other documents implicates the USPTO and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special care for declaration‑type filings relied upon by the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Filings that include declarations—e.g., TEAS Plus applications, Trademark/Service Mark Statements of Use (15 U.S.C. § 1051(d)), Combined Declarations of Use and Incontestability under Sections 8 and 15—are relied upon by the USPTO and therefore must be properly signed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order highlights that such filings are used when examining applications, registering marks, and renewing registrations; if impermissibly signed, they can lead to invalid registrations and negatively affect USPTO processes and public reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner knowledge expectation regarding laws, rules, and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners representing trademark applicants are reasonably expected to know the laws, rules, regulations, and procedures pertinent to their representation and the signature requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order states practitioners are expected to know (a) the laws, rules, regulations, and procedures pertaining to their representation of trademark clients, and (b) the potential adverse consequences to clients' intellectual property rights and to the integrity of the U.S. trademark registration system when those are violated. It cites USPTO resources (www.uspto.gov/trademarks and the TMEP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision and confirmation when delegating tasks to non‑practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: When a practitioner delegates tasks to non‑practitioner staff, the practitioner must reasonably ensure the tasks are performed in compliance with USPTO rules and guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order explains delegation is permitted but the practitioner remains responsible to confirm compliance; failing to reasonably ensure compliance (e.g., for obtaining client signatures) can constitute a violation of the duty of diligence and result in discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and enforcement: discipline, publication, and future consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the above standards may result in discipline (in this matter, a public reprimand), publication of the reprimand in the Official Gazette, and the record being considered in future disciplinary proceedings or complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agreement/Final Order modifies the Initial Decision to include a violation of § 11.103 and one charge of § 11.804(d), affirms a public reprimand, and orders publication of a notice materially consistent with the provided text. The Order also states the Office may consider the record in future matters as an aggravating factor or to rebut Respondent's statements; the Respondent in this case waived rights to seek reconsideration, review, or appeal, and to EAJA relief.
